items.title: China's Ministry of Commerce and Science Ministry propose new AI export controls including 23 AI technologies with interim pre-export registration effective immediately [ ! ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: China's First Frontier AI Export Controls: Mofcom Announcement No. 48
items.summary:
China's Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) and Ministry of Science and Technology (MOST) issued Announcement No. 48 in October 2026, proposing to add 40 technologies to the Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited or Restricted from Export, including 23 related to artificial intelligence. The announcement introduces an interim pre-export registration requirement that is already in effect, covering frontier AI model weights, agent architectures, and AI-enabled offensive cyber capabilities with specific technical thresholds.

The draft catalogue is open for public comment until November 15, 2026, while the registration requirement applies immediately to exports, including those already in progress. The controls distinguish between service access and physical export, with API and lightweight use exempted but local deployment outside China considered an export. The measures also cover licensing, ownership transfers, and intra-group code sharing, potentially affecting multinational companies. The announcement aims to prevent uncontrolled technology diffusion while allowing legitimate cooperation and is part of China's broader technology export control framework.

items.title: Proton publishes AI manifesto outlining software engineering transformation and cultural shift amid AI-driven code automation [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Proton's AI manifesto for software engineering
items.summary:
Proton has released an internal AI manifesto addressing the profound changes AI models have brought to software engineering, emphasizing the need for a cultural shift where engineers guide AI tools rather than write code manually. The manifesto highlights that traditional coding is becoming obsolete as AI can handle routine tasks, and stresses the importance of adapting quickly to remain competitive and secure in the evolving tech landscape.

The document outlines three key areas Proton must address to succeed in this transition, including changing engineer mindsets to manage AI agents effectively and improving AI autonomy. It also acknowledges the broader industry impact of AI on software development productivity and warns that failure to adapt could threaten organizational missions. Proton positions this shift as an opportunity for engineers to leverage their expertise in collaboration with AI rather than being replaced by it.

items.title: Nolan Lawson benchmarks AI-generated JavaScript frameworks using a Pokémon app to evaluate development cost, code quality, and performance across multiple frameworks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The AI cost of JavaScript frameworks
items.summary:
Nolan Lawson conducted a benchmark study to assess the AI cost of various JavaScript frameworks by instructing agents to build a small Pokémon app using different frameworks like Next.js, Nuxt, and SvelteKit. The study measured development time, token usage, lines of code, and performance and accessibility scores using Lighthouse, aiming to provide evidence-based insights into framework efficiency rather than relying on subjective developer preferences.

The experiment involved running multiple iterations per framework to account for variability in AI output and Lighthouse metrics, with a focus on a content-based app that is simple yet non-trivial. Lawson avoided specifying architecture details or CSS frameworks to keep the comparison focused on JavaScript frameworks and their meta-frameworks. The results highlight the stochastic nature of AI-generated code and the challenges in benchmarking, but offer a data-driven perspective on the trade-offs involved in choosing frameworks for AI-assisted development.

items.title: Researchers prove the Platonic Representation Hypothesis using Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs), showing models trained on different modalities learn aligned representations up to rotation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Proving and improving the Platonic Representation Hypothesis with JEPAs
items.summary: Researchers have proven the Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH), demonstrating that Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) trained on multiple modalities converge to the same representation of the world up to a rotation when trained on positive pairs representing the same scene. They show that next-token prediction is a form of JEPA with less aligned views, explaining why language models align with vision models only at large scale. The study validates these findings on datasets ranging from 145,000 captions to 940 million web images and reveals a scaling law predicting alignment efficiency, with positive views requiring significantly fewer training samples than next-token prediction to achieve similar alignment.

items.title: Researchers introduce Agentic Soft-Token Compression for long-horizon LLM agents, reducing computation by over 50% while maintaining accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: In-Model Context Compression with Agentic Soft Tokens for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
items.summary:
Researchers propose Agentic Soft-Token Compression (ASTC), a training-free method that uses soft tokens within large language model (LLM) agents to compress context in long-horizon tasks. ASTC leverages the model's native recurrent dynamics and hybrid Gated Delta Network attention to carry forward absorbed information as soft tokens, reducing later-layer computation and enabling reusable key-value caches.

Experiments show ASTC matches or exceeds the accuracy of uncompressed agents while using up to 50.68% fewer attention pairs, outperforming trained compressors that require significantly more attention pairs per successful task. This approach offers a model-native way to efficiently manage growing interaction contexts in sustained LLM tasks.

ASTC leverages the model's native recurrent dynamics and hybrid Gated Delta Network attention to carry forward absorbed information as soft tokens, reducing later-layer computation and enabling reusable key-value caches.

Experiments show ASTC matches or exceeds the accuracy of uncompressed agents while using up to 50.68% fewer attention pairs, outperforming trained compressors that require significantly more attention pairs per successful task. This approach offers a model-native way to efficiently manage growing interaction contexts in sustained LLM tasks.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.41291v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents play an important role in solving complex and sustained tasks, with ever-growing interaction contexts. However, these accumulated contexts will raise substantial computational cost and obscure key decision-relevant evidence. Existing methods typically train external compressors or context-management agents to rewrite context as shorter hard-token sequences, but such external selection may not align with the LLM's evolving representation and is necessarily lossy. In this paper, we introduce Agentic Soft-Token Compression (ASTC), a training-free compression method using soft tokens within LLM agent for long-horizon tasks. Specifically, ASTC uses the model's native recurrent dynamics to determine the already absorbed information, leveraging the commonly-used hybrid Gated Delta Network (GDN)-attention. It then carries this information forward as agentic soft tokens while retaining exact values as hard tokens. The resulting compact sequence reduces later-layer computation and yields reusable KV caches, extending the savings across the agent's trajectory. Extensive experiments on long-horizon tasks show that ASTC matches or exceeds the uncompressed agent's accuracy with up to 50.68% fewer end-to-end Attention Pairs, while trained compressors require 15.4 to 103.7 times more Attention Pairs per successful task. These findings highlight agentic soft tokens as a model-native way to carry absorbed context forward as the task representation evolves.

items.title: Researchers introduce GAIM and Q-DAIM kernel-based methods for compressing attention mechanism contexts, enabling linear-time compression and streaming updates [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Kernel-based Interpolatory Methods for Context Compression of Attention Mechanisms
items.summary: Researchers propose two novel KV-cache compression methods, GAIM and Q-DAIM, based on kernel interpolation techniques to address the quadratic complexity of attention mechanisms in language models. These methods leverage the Hilbert space formulation of attention and introduce surrogate models for linear-time compression, extending to streaming attention scenarios with adaptive interpolation updates. Numerical experiments demonstrate convergence and competitive performance on the LongBench-E benchmark, suggesting that Q-DAIM can efficiently identify key information in the KV cache for compression.
items.description: Researchers propose two novel KV-cache compression methods, GAIM and Q-DAIM, based on kernel interpolation techniques to address the quadratic complexity of attention mechanisms in language models. These methods leverage the Hilbert space formulation of attention and introduce surrogate models for linear-time compression, extending to streaming attention scenarios with adaptive interpolation updates. Numerical experiments demonstrate convergence and competitive performance on the LongBench-E benchmark, suggesting that Q-DAIM can efficiently identify key information in the KV cache for compression.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.40943v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The bottleneck of attention mechanisms, which are the fundamental building block of modern language models, is their quadratic complexity in terms of context size. There has thus been an increasing interest in the compression of the context, also called KV-cache compression. In this article, we consider the problem of compressing the context of attention mechanisms by first formulating it in the Hilbert space associated with its kernel. In this formalism, attention can be represented as the ratio of two linear maps whose interpolant is also the ratio of interpolants, this allows us to consider the interpolation of the linear maps directly. We thus introduce two novel KV-cache compression methods which we call GAIM and Q-DAIM, based on the Generalized Empirical Interpolation Method (GEIM) and the Q-Discrete Empirical Interpolation Method (Q-DEIM), respectively. As the cost of these methods is quadratic in terms of context length, we propose surrogate models based on the Taylor series, the Performer and the Random Fourier Features method which allow the compression to be done in linear time. Finally, we extend this result to the streaming attention setting, providing new methods which allow one to penalize the selection of interpolation nodes based on the previously interpolated context and to update the previous interpolation based on new information. We then provide numerical results on the convergence of the residuals and the output error in future queries and preliminary results on the LongBench-E benchmark showing performance comparable to the state-of-the-art methods. These experiments suggest that the range revealed by our Q-DAIM method could help identify where information is concentrated in the KV cache, thus enabling an efficient compression.

items.title: Researchers introduce EDB-Bio benchmark to evaluate language models' ability to assess scientific evidence in biology, showing improved calibration and efficiency after training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Do Language Models Know What Compelling Scientific Evidence Looks Like?
items.summary: Researchers developed EDB-Bio, a scientific reasoning benchmark with 96,000 episodes from drug-perturbation transcriptomics, CRISPR screens, and human genome-wide association studies, to test language models' capacity to evaluate empirical evidence and predict hypothesis validity. Initial models showed underconfidence and poor calibration, but training with proper scoring rules enhanced their performance and efficiency in sequential experiment selection tasks. The study quantifies how models update beliefs using Bayes factors and compares their judgments to expert biologists, revealing areas of agreement and bias. The work advances calibration and uncertainty analysis in scientific forecasting, with applications in cancer biology, and all related code, data, and models have been released.

Initial models showed underconfidence and poor calibration, but training with proper scoring rules enhanced their performance and efficiency in sequential experiment selection tasks. The study quantifies how models update beliefs using Bayes factors and compares their judgments to expert biologists, revealing areas of agreement and bias. The work advances calibration and uncertainty analysis in scientific forecasting, with applications in cancer biology, and all related code, data, and models have been released.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.41015v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Expert scientists excel at weighing empirical findings from multiple sources that vary in both statistical reliability and epistemic relevance. To what extent are language models, which are increasingly driving autonomous discovery systems, capable of such evidence deliberation? We introduce EDB-Bio, a scientific reasoning benchmark curated from real-world data in three biological domains: drug-perturbation transcriptomics, CRISPR screens, and human genome-wide association studies (GWAS). Each of EDB-Bio's 96k episodes presents a sequence of experimental results from published studies and asks the model to predict the probability that a target hypothesis is true. Out-of-the-box, open-weight and frontier models alike demonstrate systematic underconfidence and attain Brier scores comparable to a trivial base-rate forecaster. Post-training against strictly proper scoring rules significantly improves both calibration and discrimination. This calibration pays off downstream: in a sequential experiment selection task, our Ibis0 model is 2.5 times more efficient than the best frontier model. Throughout, quantifying evidence weights as Bayes factors reveals how models update their beliefs over time, whether they agree with expert biologists on relevance, and where they exhibit inconsistencies and biases. Our work extends calibration training and uncertainty analysis to a realistic scientific forecasting setting with applications to human cancer biology. We release all code, data, and trained models.

items.originalTitle: MUON-RT Reusing the Teacher's Trajectory for Momentum-Free Muon for LLM Self-Distillation
items.summary:
Researchers introduce Muon with Reused Teacher (Muon-RT), a method that reuses teacher-student displacement to remove momentum buffers in large language model self-distillation, reducing persistent memory requirements. Muon-RT encodes an exponentially weighted history of updates, smooths noise, and applies spectral normalization and orthogonalization to improve training efficiency.

Experiments with Self-Distillation Fine-Tuning on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct show Muon-RT improves average accuracy by 2.6 points over AdamW with 42% less memory and by 5.4 points over momentum Muon with 27% less memory. Self-Distillation Policy Optimization on Olmo-3-7B-Instruct also yields a 2.0-point accuracy improvement over AdamW.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.41104v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-distillation methods for large language models with an exponential moving average (EMA) teacher already retain a history of student updates. Muon nevertheless stores a separate momentum buffer, increasing persistent training memory. We propose Muon with Reused Teacher (Muon-RT), which reuses the teacher-student displacement to eliminate momentum buffers for hidden weight matrices. We show that this displacement encodes an exponentially weighted history of applied updates and smooths temporally uncorrelated noise under a local model. Muon-RT removes its radial component, normalizes it spectrally, and mixes it with the current gradient after Newton-Schulz (NS) orthogonalization. Under explicit regularity and alignment assumptions, we establish linear contraction of an expected objective-gap bound toward a residual error level. With Self-Distillation Fine-Tuning (SDFT) on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Muon-RT improves average accuracy over AdamW by 2.6 points with 42% less persistent memory, and over momentum Muon by 5.4 points with 27% less persistent memory. With Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO) on Olmo-3-7B-Instruct, it improves average accuracy over AdamW by 2.0 points.

items.title: SparseGDN introduces chunk-sparse linear attention with hardware-aware approximations and dynamic recurrent-event selection, achieving up to 1.94x prefill speedups on Qwen3.5 models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: SparseGDN: Chunk Sparse in Linear Attention
items.summary:
SparseGDN is a new framework that improves the efficiency of Gated Delta Networks (GDNs) for linear-time sequence modeling by combining structured intra-chunk approximations with input-dependent recurrent-event selection. It reduces computation and memory usage by selectively updating recurrent states and reconstructing token outputs from compact state snapshots, enabling outputs for every token while lowering overhead.

The approach uses a block-adjacent solver to minimize local Delta-solve computations and dynamically allocates recurrent-update budgets across attention head pairs. Evaluations on Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B models across RULER tasks with context lengths from 4K to 128K tokens show that SparseGDN retains about 29% of recurrent events on average and achieves 1.50 to 1.94 times speedups over native FLA kernels, including the cost of online selection.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.41420v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Gated Delta Networks (GDNs) offer linear-time sequence modeling, yet long-context prefill remains costly due to dense intra-chunk computation, recurrent-state updates, and intermediate state storage. We introduce SparseGDN, a hardware-aware framework that combines structured intra-chunk approximation with input-dependent recurrent-event selection while producing outputs for every token. A block-adjacent solver reduces local Delta-solve computation, while a dynamic selector allocates recurrent-update budgets across head pairs. The GPU implementation materializes updates only for selected events and reconstructs token outputs using compact state snapshots and group-local interactions, reducing computation and memory traffic. We evaluate SparseGDN on Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B across RULER tasks and context lengths from 4K to 128K. Retaining approximately 29% of recurrent events on average, SparseGDN achieves 1.50-1.94x GDN-core prefill speedups over native FLA kernels, including online selection overhead.

items.title: Researchers present TSBPO, a tree-structured policy optimization method for interactive language agents achieving over 96% success on ALFWorld and 81% on WebShop benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: TSBPO: Tree-Structured Branching for Policy Optimization in Interactive Language Agents
items.summary: Researchers introduce TSBPO, a training paradigm that addresses sampling, delayed feedback assignment, and token loss aggregation in interactive language agents within a single training loop. Using a likelihood-fitted Root/Branch allocator, TSBPO targets task continuations likely to yield contrasting outcomes under fixed rollout budgets, and applies trajectory and step advantages to compare segments and outcomes in replayed physical trees. Evaluated with a Qwen2.5-1.5B actor, TSBPO achieved 97.79% success on seen tasks and 96.64% on unseen tasks in ALFWorld, and an 81.07% per-episode success rate over six stochastic episodes for 500 WebShop test goals.
items.description: Researchers introduce TSBPO, a training paradigm that addresses sampling, delayed feedback assignment, and token loss aggregation in interactive language agents within a single training loop. Using a likelihood-fitted Root/Branch allocator, TSBPO targets task continuations likely to yield contrasting outcomes under fixed rollout budgets, and applies trajectory and step advantages to compare segments and outcomes in replayed physical trees. Evaluated with a Qwen2.5-1.5B actor, TSBPO achieved 97.79% success on seen tasks and 96.64% on unseen tasks in ALFWorld, and an 81.07% per-episode success rate over six stochastic episodes for 500 WebShop test goals.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.41697v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Training interactive language agents from terminal outcomes poses three coupled problems: which task and state continuations to sample, how to assign delayed feedback to decisions, and how to aggregate token losses for multi-token actions. We present TSBPO, a tree-structured sampling-to-update paradigm that addresses these problems within one training loop. A likelihood-fitted Root/Branch allocator uses retained task and state evidence to target continuations likely to produce contrasting terminal outcomes under fixed rollout budgets. On the resulting replayed physical trees, trajectory advantages compare immediate sibling segments, while observation-group step advantages compare outcomes at matched task/observation states. The actor then sums clipped token surrogates over each complete response and normalizes across active turns, avoiding response-length averaging in the policy-gradient term. With a Qwen2.5-1.5B actor, fixed checkpoints obtain 97.79% seen and 96.64% unseen stochastic success on ALFWorld and an 81.07% per-episode success rate over six stochastic episodes for each of the 500 WebShop test goals. A WebShop step-term ablation yields 75.93% at the same update-100 evaluation; an ALFWorld aggregation comparison shows higher observed command validity with complete-turn weighting. These results support the evaluated training configuration on two interactive benchmarks.

items.title: Researchers introduce EvoMemBench, a benchmark evaluating memory mechanisms in LLM agents across memory scope and content, comparing 15 methods under a standardized protocol [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: EvoMemBench: Benchmarking Agent Memory from a Self-Evolving Perspective
items.summary:
Researchers present EvoMemBench, a unified benchmark designed to systematically assess memory mechanisms in large language model (LLM) agents from a self-evolving perspective. The benchmark evaluates memory along two axes—memory scope (in-episode vs. cross-episode) and memory content (knowledge-oriented vs. execution-oriented)—and compares 15 representative memory methods against strong long-context baselines.

The study finds that current memory systems are not yet general solutions: long-context baselines remain competitive, memory aids most when context is insufficient or tasks are complex, and no single memory type performs consistently across all scenarios. Retrieval-based methods excel in knowledge-intensive tasks, while procedural and long-term memory methods are more effective for execution-oriented tasks when aligned with task structure. The dataset and code are publicly available to support further research on improving memory systems for LLM-based agents.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2605.18421v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent benchmarks for Large Language Model (LLM) agents mainly evaluate reasoning, planning, and execution. However, memory is also essential for agents, as it enables them to store, update, and retrieve information over time. This ability remains under-evaluated, largely because existing benchmarks do not provide a systematic way to assess memory mechanisms. In this paper, we study agent memory from a self-evolving perspective and introduce EvoMemBench, a unified benchmark organized along two axes: memory scope (in-episode vs. cross-episode) and memory content (knowledge-oriented vs. execution-oriented). We compare 15 representative memory methods with strong long-context baselines under a standardized protocol. Results show that current memory systems are still far from a general solution: long-context baselines remain highly competitive, memory helps most when the current context is insufficient or tasks are difficult, and no single memory form works consistently across all settings. Retrieval-based methods remain strong for knowledge-intensive settings, whereas procedural and long-term memory methods are more effective for execution-oriented tasks when their stored experience matches the task structure. We hope EvoMemBench facilitates future research on more effective memory systems for LLM-based agents. Our dataset and code are available at https://github.com/DSAIL-Memory/EvoMemBench.

items.title: Researchers introduce DialFork benchmark to evaluate procedural hallucination in conversational agents across 24 tasks and 12 domains [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: DialFork: Going Beyond Factuality to Evaluate Procedural Hallucination in Conversational Agents
items.summary: Researchers have developed DialFork, the first benchmark designed to measure procedural hallucination in large language model-based conversational agents, where agents produce plausible but procedurally incorrect dialogue. DialFork contains 36,278 dialogues created by forking conformant dialogues at controlled points and injecting four types of hallucinations, validated by 30 human annotators. The benchmark defines three evaluation tasks to assess procedural deviation at different granularities and proposes new dialog-flow-aware metrics, FlowKL and FlowScore, which outperform existing baselines in detecting procedural errors. DialFork is released under open licenses to encourage the community to evaluate conversational process fidelity alongside content accuracy.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.21561v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) deployed as conversational agents are increasingly expected to follow procedural logic. While factual hallucination has received extensive attention, a different failure mode has been overlooked: procedural hallucination, in which an agent produces individually fluent and factually plausible utterances while deviating from the intended conversational process. We introduce DialFork, the first benchmark to measure this failure mode on raw dialogue text. DialFork is built by forking conformant dialogues at controlled turn positions and injecting one of four hallucination types, yielding 36,278 dialogues across 24 tasks in 12 domains; 30 human annotators validate the construction. We define three evaluation tasks that characterize procedural deviation at three granularities: how far a set of dialogues deviates from conformant ones (monitoring deployed agents), how far a single dialogue does (procedural retrieval), and at which turn a dialogue first goes off-track (real-time guardrails). For the first two, we propose dialog-flow-aware metrics, FlowKL and FlowScore, that compare dialogues by how they unfold rather than their content. At the dialogue level, FlowScore significantly outperforms all baselines across seven encoders, showing that semantic similarity is no substitute for procedural similarity. We release DialFork under open licenses at https://github.com/idiap/dialfork, hoping the community will measure conversational process alongside content.

items.title: Researchers present AnytimeReasoner framework with Budget Relative Policy Optimization to improve token efficiency and reasoning flexibility in large language models under varying token budgets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Optimizing Anytime Reasoning via Budget Relative Policy Optimization
items.summary:
Researchers introduce AnytimeReasoner, a framework designed to optimize anytime reasoning performance in large language models by improving token efficiency and enabling flexible reasoning under different token budget constraints. The approach involves truncating reasoning processes to fit sampled token budgets and summarizing optimal answers for verification, which provides dense rewards for reinforcement learning optimization. They also propose Budget Relative Policy Optimization (BRPO), a variance reduction technique to enhance learning robustness and efficiency.

Empirical tests on mathematical reasoning tasks show that AnytimeReasoner consistently outperforms existing methods like GRPO across various token budgets and prior distributions, improving both training and token efficiency. This work addresses limitations of prior reinforcement learning approaches that optimize only final performance under fixed large token budgets, offering a more adaptable and efficient solution for scaling reasoning capabilities in large language models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2505.13438v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Scaling test-time compute is crucial for enhancing the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). Existing approaches typically employ reinforcement learning (RL) to maximize a verifiable reward obtained at the end of reasoning traces. However, such methods optimize only the final performance under a large and fixed token budget, which hinders efficiency in both training and deployment. In this work, we present a novel framework, AnytimeReasoner, to optimize anytime reasoning performance, which aims to improve token efficiency and the flexibility of reasoning under varying token budget constraints. To achieve this, we truncate the complete thinking process to fit within sampled token budgets from a prior distribution, compelling the model to summarize the optimal answer for each truncated thinking for verification. This introduces verifiable dense rewards into the reasoning process, facilitating more effective credit assignment in RL optimization. We then optimize the thinking and summary policies in a decoupled manner to maximize the cumulative reward. Additionally, we introduce a novel variance reduction technique, Budget Relative Policy Optimization (BRPO), to enhance the robustness and efficiency of the learning process when reinforcing the thinking policy. Empirical results in mathematical reasoning tasks demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms GRPO across all thinking budgets under various prior distributions, enhancing both training and token efficiency.

items.title: Researchers introduce Mstar, a method that evolves task-specific memory programs for large language model agents, improving performance across conversation, embodied planning, and expert reasoning tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: M$^\star$: Every Task Deserves Its Own Memory Harness
items.summary: Researchers present Mstar, a method that automatically discovers optimized memory harnesses for large language model agents by evolving executable Python memory programs tailored to specific tasks. Mstar jointly optimizes components defining memory schema, logic, and instructions to better handle diverse requirements such as conversation, embodied planning, and specialized reasoning. Evaluations on four distinct tasks show that Mstar outperforms existing baselines and produces structurally distinct memory programs suited to each domain. These results suggest that customizing memory harnesses per task enhances agent performance and that memory-program search is an effective approach to achieve this.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2604.11811v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language model agents rely on a memory harness to write, organize, retrieve, and use past experience. A harness that works for one task often fails on another, because conversations, embodied planning, and expert reasoning require different storage and retrieval behavior. To address this limitation, we introduce Mstar, a method that automatically discovers task-optimized memory programs through reflective code evolution. Specifically, Mstar operationalizes a memory harness as an executable Python memory program that defines the Schema, Logic, and Instruction, and optimizes these components jointly. We evaluate Mstar on four tasks covering conversation, embodied planning, and specialized reasoning. Our results demonstrate that Mstar improves performance over existing baselines across all evaluated tasks. Furthermore, the evolved memory programs exhibit structurally distinct processing mechanisms for each evaluated domain. These findings suggest that every task benefits from its own memory harness, and that memory-program search provides a concrete way to discover it.

items.title: Researchers formalize controllable user simulation as a causal inference problem to improve evaluation of conversational agents and propose methods to eliminate bias and preserve behavioral diversity [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Controllable User Simulation
items.summary: Researchers address limitations in evaluating conversational agents using offline datasets by formalizing controllable user simulation as a causal inference problem. They identify that standard training methods introduce look-ahead bias linked to the behavior policy, causing evaluation metric variance to explode under policy shifts, a phenomenon termed controllability collapse. To fix this, they propose theoretical conditions and practical training methods including a priori controls, step-wise dynamic controls, and policy-conditioned learning. Empirical results show their approach removes bias, maintains natural variance, and generalizes well to unseen agent behaviors, unlike standard global controls that distort distributions and reduce diversity.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2605.11519v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Using offline datasets to evaluate conversational agents often fails to cover rare scenarios or to support testing new policies. This has motivated the use of controllable user simulators for targeted, counterfactual evaluation, typically implemented by prompting or fine-tuning large language models. In this work, we formalize controllable simulation as a causal inference problem. By bridging natural language evaluation with off-policy evaluation methodology, we show that the standard practice of training simulators via supervised fine-tuning on post-hoc trajectory labels yields a structurally biased model. Specifically, these labels are inextricably coupled to the data-generating behavior policy, injecting a look-ahead bias that breaks causal consistency. Furthermore, we prove that under policy shift this failure causes the variance of evaluation metrics to explode geometrically, a phenomenon we term controllability collapse. To restore causal consistency, we establish theoretical conditions for accurate simulation and propose practical training mitigations: a priori controls, step-wise dynamic controls, and direct policy-conditioned learning. Empirical evaluation confirms that while standard global controls distort conversational distributions and collapse behavioral diversity, our causally grounded simulators eliminate look-ahead bias, preserve natural variance, and exhibit robust zero-shot generalization to unseen agent behaviors.

items.title: SIRF model internalizes complex platform policies for industrial content risk control, achieving 71.3% Black Recall@P95 with low latency and improved mis-penalization recovery [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: SIRF: A Spec-Internalized Risk Foundation Model for Industrial Content Risk Control
items.summary:
SIRF (Spec-Internalized Risk Foundation Model) is designed for industrial content risk control, focusing on high precision and second-level latency rather than average accuracy. It internalizes complex platform policies into model weights through continued pretraining without additional human annotation, enabling ultra-low-latency, verdict-only deployment that applies rules precisely.

A controlled comparison with a baseline model shows SIRF-8B-SFT improves Black Recall@P95 by 15.1 percentage points using about 70 million continued pretraining tokens, without reducing general ability. Deployed as a tree-model adjudication layer, SIRF recovers 20% more mis-penalized samples and reduces mis-penalization by approximately 70% in freezing scenarios, demonstrating effective policy internalization and transfer at low cost.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2609.11752v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: For industrial content risk control, the real deployment constraint is not average accuracy but how much risk can be auto-handled under high precision and second-level latency. We present SIRF (Spec-Internalized Risk Foundation Model), which internalizes a platform's complex policies, synthesized without additional human annotation via EntiGraph, MAGA rewriting and account-level chain-of-thought (CoT), into the weights via continued pretraining (CPT), so rules are applied at high precision under an ultra-low-latency, verdict-only deployment. A controlled same-source comparison (Qwen3-8B-SFT vs. SIRF-8B-SFT, identical policy injection and verdict-only output form, differing only in policy-grounded CPT) attributes the gain to internalization: SIRF-8B-SFT reaches 71.3% Black Recall@P95, +15.1pp over the baseline, using only ~70M CPT tokens without harming general ability, and among included, logprob-available models under this interface it matches or exceeds far larger systems. SIRF is deployed as a tree-model adjudication layer (20% more mis-penalized samples recovered) and transfers to a freezing scenario at low cost (~70% relative mis-penalization reduction).

items.title: Researchers introduce a unified four-coefficient per-token gating parameterization for on-policy knowledge distillation, combining forward and reverse KL losses with multi-channel and bias terms [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A Unified Per-Token Gating Family for On-Policy Distillation: FKL/RKL Mixing with Multi-Channel and Bias Coefficients
items.summary: Researchers propose a new four-coefficient parameterization for per-token gating in on-policy knowledge distillation (OPD), unifying existing methods like EOPD and ToDi by allowing multi-channel composition and explicit bias. Experiments on TweetEval tasks using a Qwen3-32B teacher and Qwen3-4B student show that configurations within this family outperform single-channel gating approaches in most cases. The study presents this parameterization as a shared framework for comparing per-token gating designs in short-output classification OPD, supported by exploratory aggregate evidence and targeted replications that are directionally consistent but not statistically significant at small sample sizes.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2609.11768v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Per-token gating of forward/reverse KL losses has become a standard technique for on-policy knowledge distillation (OPD), but existing methods such as EOPD (Jin et al., 2026) and ToDi (Jung et al., 2025) each fix a single gating signal and a single gating direction, and the two have never been compared directly. We introduce a four-coefficient parameterization lambda_t = sigma(a * h_t + b * u(x) + c + d * gap_t) in which direction-aligned proxies of EOPD and ToDi appear as one-dimensional (1D) restrictions, and which adds multi-channel composition and an explicit bias as further degrees of freedom. On TweetEval (Barbieri et al., 2020) emotion and hate, with a Qwen3-32B teacher and a Qwen3-4B student, configurations in the full family reach higher accuracy than the matched-magnitude single-channel (entropy-only / gap-only) 1D restrictions in 33 of 36 comparable cells, and a 26-cell mean-match isolation experiment places dynamic gating ahead of effective-KL-matched static baselines in 19 of 26 cells. Because cells share training data, models, and parameter substructure, we report both counts as exploratory aggregate directional evidence rather than as independent hypothesis tests. Targeted three-seed paired replications of the nine headline comparisons singled out by that sweep -- including a third task, offensive -- are directionally consistent, but individually smaller than the single-seed estimates and not significant at n=3. We therefore present the parameterization primarily as a shared coordinate system for comparing per-token gating designs in short-output classification OPD.

items.title: Researchers report three preregistered studies analyzing harness effects on a longevity-tuned 1.7B language model, finding mixed gains mostly linked to unparsed data and constant label baselines [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: What Does a Harness Repair? Three Preregistered Studies Around a Longevity-Tuned Language Model
items.summary:
Researchers conducted three preregistered studies to evaluate the impact of harnesses on a frozen longevity-tuned 1.7 billion parameter language model. They found that reported performance gains often stemmed from unparsed input rows and that replication attempts missed these effects. Across various tests, harnesses sometimes improved accuracy over capped settings but were often comparable to constant answer baselines or simpler methods.

The studies included evaluations on different model sizes and tasks, such as mortality prediction and question answering benchmarks. Some harnesses outperformed others in specific settings, but overall gains were inconsistent and frequently aligned with label distribution biases rather than meaningful improvements. The findings suggest that harness benefits depend on task characteristics and label skew, with no clear advantage demonstrated across all question types or models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.05533v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A harness search around a frozen longevity-tuned 1.7B model reported a rescue. An audit found that the gain came from rows the start left unparsed, that the caller sent each row's reference answer as an assistant turn, and that replication through the same pipeline missed it. Is a harness's gain more than a constant answer would give? We preregistered three studies and report every endpoint. In the first two, thinking off raised test accuracy over a capped thinking setting in 7 of 12 cells, mostly on rows the cap left unparsed. It was not meaningfully worse than a rescue in 7 of 9 small-model test cells or than four GEPA harnesses at 1.7B. Replication reproduced an injected defect's distortion in 9 of 20 evaluable cases (7 fixed by design). At 14B, two GEPA harnesses beat thinking off by 34 points on test but were not detectably above the strongest constant label, and answered "Yes" in 94.6% and 98.2% of parsed mortality answers on test. In the third study (SmolLM3-3B, base Qwen3-1.7B), GEPA beat the constant on FPB (confirmatory, both partitions); thinking off was not meaningfully worse than any BoolQ harness, and 3 of 4 MMLU-Pro searches kept their seed (the fourth inconclusive on test). On Autocast (exploratory), the harnesses were within 0.7 points of the constant and gave one label in 93.1% to 96.8% of parsed answers, both on test. On questions about the input or about knowledge (FPB, BoolQ, MMLU-Pro), GEPA beat the constant or found no clear gain over thinking off; on questions that ask for a prediction (14B mortality, descriptive; Autocast, exploratory), the harness ended near the constant and gave one label almost throughout while its gain over thinking off looked large. The constant label told the two apart wherever the gain was large. This rests on few tasks that also differ in label skew, number of labels and task type, so it is not shown to depend on the kind of question.

items.originalTitle: The agentic web is here
items.summary:
In 2001, Tim Berners-Lee and colleagues proposed the Semantic Web, envisioning autonomous software agents navigating the internet to fulfill user needs without manual browsing. While the original idea required extensive tagging of web content and did not gain traction, recent advances in large language models have enabled AI agents to understand and interact with web content autonomously, fulfilling Berners-Lee's vision in new ways.

Today, AI agents such as Meta's Muse, OpenAI's Dots, and Anthropic's Claude Duet are widely used to perform tasks like booking appointments and searching for information, changing how users engage with the web. This emerging "agentic web" is reshaping online experiences, with companies adapting content and services for agent interaction, though its long-term impact on web openness and control remains uncertain.

items.title: Ryanair considers pay freezes, reducing flight crew, and increasing AI use to offset €2bn fuel cost rise amid Middle East conflict [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Ryanair consider pay freezes, AI and reducing crew on flights as fuel costs soar
items.summary:
Ryanair is evaluating cost-cutting measures including pay freezes, reducing the number of crew members on flights, and expanding the use of artificial intelligence to manage soaring fuel costs driven by the Middle East conflict. The airline expects its jet fuel expenses to increase by about €2 billion in the financial year ending March 2028, with European short-haul fares likely to rise by up to 20% as a result.

The company said 80% of its fuel needs until March are hedged at $67 per barrel, but only 25% of the following year's requirements are hedged at $95 per barrel. Ryanair's CEO Michael O’Leary noted that while fare increases and competitor capacity reductions may offset some costs, they will not fully cover the fuel bill rise. The airline reported a 6% year-on-year profit decline to €1.61 billion in the quarter ending September, with passenger numbers growing 5% to 64.5 million.

items.title: Roblox reports over 70,000 AI-generated games published in five months as Steam acknowledges challenges with AI content quality [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Roblox embraces AI-generated games as Steam raises concerns about quality
items.summary:
Roblox has embraced AI-powered game development, launching its Build tool in July 2026 and enabling users to publish more than 70,000 games within five months. The company highlights rapid content creation and increased use of AI tools among top creators, positioning itself to capture a significant share of the global gaming market.

In contrast, Valve has acknowledged issues with low-quality AI-generated games flooding its Steam platform but has yet to find a solution. Roblox emphasizes its social distribution model as a way to help quality content reach audiences despite the surge in AI-generated games, while also introducing initiatives to make games playable across devices and platforms.

items.originalTitle: Haas: Postgres 19 is late, and it's AI's fault
items.summary: Haas has stated that the release of PostgreSQL 19 has been delayed, attributing the delay to the project's emphasis on quality and the challenges posed by artificial intelligence technologies in identifying long-standing bugs. The delay is considered short-term and not particularly concerning in the broader context of the project's goals. He highlighted that AI, particularly large language models, can uncover bugs that humans missed over the past forty years, raising questions about how PostgreSQL will continue to innovate and catch up with these findings. Haas and others are actively working to address these challenges and determine the project's future direction.

items.title: Sam Altman says running AI models locally wastes limited DRAM resources amid ongoing memory shortages [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Sam Altman on Local AI
items.summary:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman criticized the trend of running AI models locally on personal devices, arguing it inefficiently uses scarce DRAM memory that could be better utilized in cloud data centers. He highlighted that local AI setups often use only a small fraction of their memory capacity, exacerbating a global memory shortage expected to continue through 2030.

Altman contrasted his view with partners like Nvidia and Microsoft, who promote local AI for privacy and reduced cloud dependence. He also noted that memory manufacturers are cautious about expanding production due to past overcapacity risks, contributing to the current supply constraints. The shortage has made AI-optimized PCs expensive, limiting mainstream adoption until prices decrease.

items.title: Researchers propose Li2SAO, a lightweight asynchronous RL optimization method with group-relative actor-critic bootstrapping, improving early training and performance over GRPO and LiSAO on agentic tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Li$^{2}$SAO: Lifting Light Singl-Rollout Asynchronous RL Optimization via Group-Relative Actor-Critic Bootstrapping
items.summary:
Asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) is increasingly used for post-training large language models to improve efficiency by updating models as rollouts arrive. Recent methods like Single-rollout Asynchronous Optimization (SAO) improve stability but rely on closed-source pretrained value models. This paper introduces LiSAO, a lightweight SAO variant without pretrained value models, and finds it underperforms GRPO on reasoning tasks but excels on agentic tasks, though it lags in early training due to an untrained value model.

To address early training limitations, the authors propose Li2SAO, which uses group-relative actor-critic bootstrapping: training the actor with group-relative advantage and the critic with group-centered returns before switching to single-rollout generalized advantage estimation. Experiments show Li2SAO matches or surpasses GRPO early in training and achieves higher final performance. The code is publicly available.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.40726v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) is becoming a mainstream paradigm for post-training large language models (LLMs), as it improves training efficiency by updating the model as rollouts arrive. Recent work argues that group-wise sampling in GRPO does not naturally fit asynchronous RL training because rollout lengths follow a long-tailed distribution, and proposes Single-rollout Asynchronous Optimization (SAO) to improve stability and off-policy behavior, especially on agentic tasks. However, SAO relies on a closed-source value model obtained from scaling value pretraining. In this paper, we analyze GRPO and LiSAO, our lightweight reproduction of SAO without the pretrained value model, on single-turn reasoning and multi-turn agentic tasks. We find that GRPO outperforms LiSAO on reasoning tasks, while the reverse holds on agentic tasks. Since the value model of LiSAO is not yet well trained , LiSAO lags behind GRPO substantially in early training steps. To address this issue, we propose Li$^{2}$SAO, which Lifts Light Single-rollout Asynchronous Optimization with group-relative actor-critic bootstrapping: while the critic is cold, a group-relative advantage trains the actor and a group-centered return trains the critic, after which training switches to single-rollout GAE. Experiments show that Li$^{2}$SAO catches up with or surpasses GRPO in early training and further raises the later performance ceiling. Code is available at https://github.com/jd-cc-coder/Li2SAO.

items.title: Researchers present Mage-VL-Cowork, a 4B-parameter hybrid computer-use agent trained via a five-stage curriculum using evolved teacher harnesses and skill-conditioned workflows [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Mage-VL-Cowork: A Full Training Recipe to Learn Hybrid Computer Use From Evolved Harnesses
items.summary:
Mage-VL-Cowork integrates visual GUI interaction with code and terminal execution in a single policy, trained from a multimodal checkpoint through midtraining, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning. The training uses Mage-CUA-Forge to generate over 293,000 desktop and web tasks across nearly 7,000 skills, reducing per-task costs by 82.6% through reusable workflows and application-specific preparers.

Instead of distilling a fixed teacher model, the team evolved teacher harnesses and specialized agent harnesses to produce high-quality training trajectories with stage-specific supervision. Mage-VL-Cowork-4B achieved 66.0% accuracy on the OSWorld-Verified benchmark with efficient reasoning costs, setting a new state-of-the-art for its parameter size and advancing on-device AI capabilities.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.40747v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Effective computer-use agents (CUAs) should seamlessly combine visual GUI interaction with code and terminal execution within a single policy. We present Mage-VL-Cowork, a 4B hybrid CUA trained from a general multimodally aligned checkpoint through an end-to-end, progressive five-stage curriculum across midtraining, SFT, and RL. To power this curriculum at scale, Mage-CUA-Forge replaces per-task agent construction with reusable, skill-conditioned generation workflows and application-specific preparers, synthesizing 293,806 desktop and web tasks across 6,915 skills while reducing recurring per-task expenditure by 82.6%. Rather than directly distilling a default teacher, we evolve the teacher harness and instantiate specialized CUA harnesses to yield high-quality trajectories alongside stage-specific supervision. Mage-VL-Cowork-4B finally climbs to 66.0% on OSWorld-Verified through different training stages with more efficient reasoning cost, achieving state-of-the-art performance at its parameter size and pushing forward the frontier of on-device intelligence.

items.title: Researchers compare continuous diffusion language models and speculative drafters for unconditional text generation, finding LangFlow outperforms DSpark variants on longer sequences [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Generative Gap Between Speculative Drafter and Continuous Diffusion Language Model
items.summary: Researchers compared continuous diffusion language models (CDLMs) and speculative drafters by training LangFlow and DSpark architectures from scratch on unconditional OpenWebText generation at sequence lengths of 16, 128, and 1024 tokens without verification. They evaluated generation perplexity and distributional similarity, finding LangFlow outperforms DSpark variants at lengths 128 and 1024, while DSpark-RNN leads at length 16. The study highlights iterative full-sequence refinement as a key factor in LangFlow's advantage on longer sequences, despite improvements from recurrent memory in DSpark models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.40847v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Continuous diffusion language models (CDLMs) and speculative drafters offer efficient language generation but are typically evaluated differently: CDLMs generate independently through iterative refinement, whereas drafters propose text for target-model verification and correction. We compare their architectures without verification, using LangFlow for CDLMs and adapting DSpark's Markov and recurrent-head architectures for standalone generation. All models are trained from scratch for unconditional, single-block OpenWebText generation at lengths 16, 128, and 1024, without target features or verification, using common preprocessing, backbone dimensions, and training-update budgets. We evaluate generation perplexity (GenPPL) with an external language model and distributional similarity to reference text with MAUVE. With default denoising steps equal to sequence length, LangFlow outperforms both DSpark variants on both metrics at lengths 128 and 1024, while DSpark-RNN leads at 16. A conditional KL analysis characterizes dependencies excluded by the Markov head's previous-token conditioning. Recurrent memory removes this restriction and improves both metrics, but the longer-sequence gap persists. Teacher probability matching further lowers Markov GenPPL without observed MAUVE gains. Increasing LangFlow's denoising steps at fixed weights improves both metrics at lengths 16 and 128, changing the length-128 ordering relative to DSpark-RNN. These results establish LangFlow's longer-sequence advantage under the evaluated budgets and highlight iterative full-sequence refinement as a route to improving standalone generation beyond gains from recurrent head memory.

items.title: Researchers find pruning redundant attention heads in GPT-2-XL reduces verbatim memorisation by 91.5% while improving language modeling performance [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Fewer Heads, Fewer Memories: Pruning Redundant Attention Heads Suppresses Verbatim Memorisation
items.summary: A study shows that zeroing out a large number of redundant attention heads in the GPT-2-XL language model significantly suppresses its tendency to reproduce memorised sequences from training data, reducing memorisation by 91.5%. This pruning also improves the model's performance on the WikiText-103 benchmark, lowering perplexity by 0.92, suggesting that many attention heads are unnecessary for downstream tasks. The findings indicate that attention-head redundancy can be exploited at inference time to mitigate privacy and intellectual property risks without retraining or altering the training data.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.40974v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models have been shown to memorise and reproduce verbatim sequences from their training data, raising concerns about privacy leakage, intellectual property exposure, and the limits of generalisation. Recent theoretical work suggests that attention heads may contribute to this behaviour by functioning as associative memory mechanisms, with memorisation capacity scaling with the number of heads. At the same time, empirical work has shown that many attention heads are redundant and can be pruned with limited impact on downstream performance. Despite these parallel findings, the effect of pruning redundant heads on memorised-sequence reproduction remains unexplored. In this work, we demonstrate that zeroing out a substantial fraction of attention heads prior to inference can significantly suppress verbatim memorisation while preserving, or even improving, language modelling performance on the benchmark used to identify redundant heads. Evaluating GPT-2-XL(1.5B) on known memorised sequences, we find that pruning 729 task-redundant heads reduces the memorisation count by 91.5%, while improving WikiText-103 perplexity by 0.92. These findings suggest that attention-head redundancy can be exploited to mitigate memorisation at inference time, without retraining or modifying the training data.

items.title: Researchers introduce BlindToChange benchmark showing AI agents often fail to proactively detect recent real-world changes affecting their responses [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: BlindToChange: AI Agents Can Find Changes When Asked But Do They Look When Needed?
items.summary: Researchers have developed BlindToChange, a benchmark designed to evaluate whether AI agents proactively discover recent events that impact their outputs without explicit user prompts. The study finds that while AI agents can find recent changes when directly asked, their performance drops significantly—by up to 27.5 points—when such changes are not explicitly mentioned in user requests. This gap highlights that many agents do not verify if relevant facts have changed, leading to incorrect or outdated responses. BlindToChange uses real-world events drawn from Wikidata and focuses on recommendation tasks where obvious options are invalidated by recent developments. The benchmark aims to track progress in AI systems' ability to account for recent, implicitly relevant information in their responses.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.41435v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Given that AI agents can search the web broadly and deeply in real time, it is tempting to conclude that their outputs account for recent world events. We show that this conclusion does not hold in practice. While agents can search and easily find recent changes, the correctness of their responses depends on whether they search and what they search for. Popular agentic search benchmarks like BrowseComp cannot expose failures wherein agents do not recognize their own assumptions that should be verified, since these benchmarks explicitly state what needs to be found. In contrast, many user requests state only the final information need (e.g., an itinerary for a trip), leaving the agent to discover relevant changes (e.g., the temporary closure of a museum) and account for their consequences. To highlight such gaps, we introduce BlindToChange, a benchmark that measures whether agents proactively discover recent events that affect their responses. Our benchmark comprises requests for recommendations where an obvious candidate is no longer applicable due to a recent real-world event. These events are drawn automatically from Wikidata, allowing BlindToChange to be periodically refreshed. Strikingly, we find a big gap -- as high as 27.5 points, even at high reasoning effort -- in systems' performance, when the recent event is not explicitly mentioned compared to when we ask about it directly. Analyzing search trajectories, we learn that more than half of the failures can be attributed to the fact that agents do not directly search to verify whether a relevant fact has changed. Our benchmark highlights, and tracks, a new axis of progress, wherein systems account for recent information that is not explicitly mentioned in the user request.

items.title: Researchers trace fine-tuned language model behaviors to KV cache patches, showing transfer and removal of behaviors via attention mechanism [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: KV-Cache Patching: Tracing How and Where Fine-Tuned Behaviors Arise
items.summary:
Researchers investigate where fine-tuned behaviors in language models arise by patching the key-value (KV) cache from a LoRA fine-tuned model into the base model and vice versa. They find that some behaviors, such as responding in German or emergent misalignment, can be transferred or removed through KV cache patching, indicating that altered processing of previous tokens via attention contributes to fine-tuned responses.

The study reveals that the impact of patching increases with the amount of KV cache replaced and is concentrated at pivotal token positions, particularly system-prompt and chat-template tokens, which have disproportionate influence on model behavior.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.41480v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fine-tuning a language model changes how it responds, but where is this fine-tuned behavior instantiated? To better understand this, we evaluate whether the change in model behavior arises only during the generation of the answer tokens where the change manifests, or whether altered processing of previous tokens causes it via the attention mechanism. For this, we patch the KV cache from a LoRA fine-tuned model into the unmodified base model, and vice versa. Our results show that for some behaviors, like responding in German or emergent misalignment, patching the KV cache can indeed transfer them from the fine-tuned to the base model. Correspondingly, patching the KV cache from base to fine-tune can partially or fully remove fine-tuned behavior. Furthermore, we find that the effect of patching grows with how much of the KV cache is patched and concentrates at a few pivotal positions, with system-prompt and chat-template tokens having disproportionate influence.

items.title: Researchers present KEEPER, a method analyzing control-sufficient textual memory for long-horizon LLM agents, highlighting error persistence and reward-related prediction's impact on task performance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: KEEPER: Learning Control-Sufficient Textual Memory for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
items.summary:
Researchers introduce KEEPER, a framework evaluating four auxiliary objectives for recursive textual memory in long-horizon large language model (LLM) agents, focusing on how supervision targets affect agent performance. They identify self-consistency bias as the persistence of incorrect claims in memory and find that reward-related prediction objectives yield the highest task performance before and after offline reinforcement learning, outperforming joint supervision.

The study includes a claim-level analysis showing that errors can persist despite corrective observations, emphasizing the need to assess error persistence and valid information retention alongside task outcomes. This work suggests that task performance alone does not guarantee reliable memory updates in LLM agents and proposes metrics to better evaluate memory reliability.

We define self-consistency bias as the persistence of incorrect claims already present in the incoming memory. We present KEEPER, a comparative analysis of four auxiliary objectives along information-content and update-sensitivity axes within a shared recursive interface, examining how supervision targets relate to agent performance. A claim-level analysis of one baseline trajectory documents error persistence despite corrective observations. Together, these analyses motivate evaluating error persistence and valid-information retention alongside task outcomes.

items.title: Researchers propose DualBudget sparse-expert diffusion model balancing attention graph edges and expert activation for long-context text tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Sparse Text Diffusion under Dual Budgets: Context Connectivity and Expert Activation
items.summary: Researchers introduce DualBudget, a sparse-expert diffusion configuration that manages two separate computational budgets—attention graph edges and expert activations per token—to improve long-context text processing. The model connects various attention mechanisms with conditional expert computation and is evaluated on tasks including scientific summarization, multi-hop question answering, dialogue, and sentence-pair prediction. The study shows performance gains over baselines up to 16,000 tokens with some degradation at longer lengths and reports a 20% cost reduction compared to DiffuSeq under an unspecified timing convention. Ablation studies reveal mixed effects on evaluation metrics, and the analysis distinguishes measured results from unverified claims about training speed, global coherence, and deployment memory.

We specify normalized masked attention, distinguish denoising depth from sampling iterations, and derive graph and compute bounds. A reported sparse-expert configuration, denoted DualBudget, is analyzed across scientific summarization, multi-hop question answering, dialogue, and sentence-pair prediction. All supplied table measurements are retained. The length study shows gains over the listed baselines through 16K, together with measurable degradation as length increases. Ablations reveal mixed changes across the three reported scores, while the cost record indicates a 20% reduction relative to DiffuSeq under an unspecified timing convention. The analysis separates these observations from unmeasured claims about training speed, absorbing states, global coherence, and deployment memory.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.41574v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Unlike autoregressive (AR) models, diffusion language models (DLMs) permit parallel token updates, flexible generation, and bidirectional attention, but leading systems rely on costly pretraining or full-model fine-tuning. We present Build Your Own DLM (BYOD), a generalizable LoRA-only recipe for parameter-efficient AR-to-DLM conversion. Without architecture-specific tuning, BYOD induces diffusion generation in Gemma 2 9B, Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen2.5 7B, and Ministral 8B; to our knowledge, this is the first reported AR-to-DLM conversion of a Mistral model. The adapters comprise 4.1-5.8% of final parameters while every base-model parameter remains frozen; each 25,000-iteration conversion needs at most 102.4M tokens, processed in 3.1-4.0 hours on one Google Colab GPU. All four models generate from fully masked sequences, use bidirectional context in a controlled attention test, and retain substantial parent-model knowledge. BYOD-Gemma is the strongest BYOD conversion on our nine-task evaluation, reaching 50.6% average accuracy compared with 51.9% for LLaDA 8B Instruct in the same harness. Open-generation quality at low network function evaluation (NFE) budgets remains the principal limitation: BYOD perplexity is 8.3-11.1 versus 4.1 for LLaDA and 2.2-3.0 for the AR parents when generating 128 tokens in 64 steps. To enable further experimentation and inspection, we provide a standalone training and evaluation implementation and interactive demos for all four conversions. BYOD thus provides a practical route for extending diffusion generation to other existing model families while identifying the gap that efficient conversion must next close.

items.title: Researchers identify unintended discourse changes caused by activation steering in large language models and propose a vector-based intervention to restore discourse while preserving intended behavior [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When Steering Shifts Discourse: Identifying and Intervening on Discourse-Level Changes due to Activation Steering in LLMs
items.summary: Activation steering is a technique that modifies large language model outputs by adding vectors to their activations during inference, aiming to control behavior or tone without retraining. Researchers found that this method also causes significant unintended changes in discourse aspects such as formality, evidence use, and ambiguity, which prior work only measured through coarse metrics like perplexity. They developed a complementary vector intervention that counteracts these unintended discourse shifts, restoring about 78% of the changes while maintaining the intended steering effects in approximately 93% of cases.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.41661v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Activation steering is an inference-time technique used to control or modify the behavior, tone, or safety properties of a large language model (LLM) without retraining the model's weights or editing its input prompt, but simply by adding a vector to its residual-stream activations. However, activation steering also changes the generated text in unintended ways, unrelated to intended behavior change, that are not well understood. Prior work has measured these changes only through coarse signals such as perplexity. In this work, we show that steering systematically produces significant changes in discourse dimensions of the generated text, such as its formality, use of evidence, and ambiguity. We present a way of countering this by adding a second, complementary vector that targets the affected discourse dimension. This intervention restores about 78% of the unintended discourse changes while preserving the intended steering behavior in about 93% of the generations.

items.title: Researchers introduce PEEL to extract taxonomic hierarchies from Matryoshka Representation Learning embeddings, recovering ontological structures without task-specific training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Peeling the Matryoshka: Extracting Ontological Structure from Retrieval Embeddings
items.summary: Researchers present PEEL (Peeling Embeddings to Extract Latent ontologies), a minimal probe that decodes hierarchical taxonomic structures from frozen Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) embeddings by leveraging an order-embedding objective and minimum spanning arborescence. This method recovers taxonomic directed acyclic graphs with high fidelity on two benchmarks and transfers to new domains without target-edge supervision, using only concept vocabularies and no documents. The study finds that prefix lengths in MRL embeddings correspond to coarse-to-fine granularity in taxonomies, a pattern consistent across three distinct MRL models. PEEL offers a cost-effective alternative to clustering and large language model-based taxonomy construction methods, which require extensive tuning or expensive training.
items.description: Researchers present PEEL (Peeling Embeddings to Extract Latent ontologies), a minimal probe that decodes hierarchical taxonomic structures from frozen Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) embeddings by leveraging an order-embedding objective and minimum spanning arborescence. This method recovers taxonomic directed acyclic graphs with high fidelity on two benchmarks and transfers to new domains without target-edge supervision, using only concept vocabularies and no documents. The study finds that prefix lengths in MRL embeddings correspond to coarse-to-fine granularity in taxonomies, a pattern consistent across three distinct MRL models. PEEL offers a cost-effective alternative to clustering and large language model-based taxonomy construction methods, which require extensive tuning or expensive training.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.41785v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Taxonomy construction is essential for knowledge-intensive NLP yet remains costly: clustering-based methods (i) need careful per-corpus tuning and yield unstable hierarchies, while LLM-based pipelines (ii) depend on expensive task-specific training that does not transfer across domains. We report an empirical finding that bears on both: in Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) embeddings, where each leading prefix is itself a usable, coarser vector, prefix length aligns with the coarse-to-fine granularity of gold taxonomies; shuffled- and reverse-dimension controls isolate the alignment to the learned early prefix dimensions. The pattern holds across three architecturally distinct MRL models. To test whether this regularity is usable, we introduce PEEL (Peeling Embeddings to Extract Latent ontologies): a minimal probe over these frozen embeddings, trained once with an order-embedding objective that represents hierarchy as vector containment; a minimum spanning arborescence then decodes taxonomic DAGs. Using only a concept vocabulary (no documents), PEEL recovers taxonomic DAGs with high structural fidelity on two OLLM benchmarks, transferring to a new domain with no target-edge supervision. The end-to-end OLLM pipeline, which jointly discovers concepts and induces structure from document corpora, is reported as a cross-task reference. Pre-trained retrieval embeddings encode a decodable granularity gradient; a minimal probe renders it as explicit parent-child (is-a) structure.

items.title: SimXAI introduces a lightweight LLM-based conversational layer that improves interaction quality and understanding in conversational explainable AI by replacing traditional modular pipelines [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: SimXAI: A Simple Drop-in Layer Increases Interaction Quality and Understanding in Conversational XAI
items.summary:
SimXAI is a new conversational layer designed for explainable AI (XAI) agents that replaces separate modules for intent recognition, dialogue management, and response generation with a single large language model (LLM) that accesses existing XAI resources. This approach aims to improve handling of context-dependent follow-up questions while maintaining faithfulness to underlying XAI methods.

The researchers developed an evaluation suite to test parsing accuracy, faithfulness, and contextualization across multiple datasets, where SimXAI demonstrated strong function-selection accuracy and better contextual understanding. In a user study replacing the conversational layer of a representative GUS-based agent, users completed tasks more accurately and with fewer conversational turns, indicating improved conversational quality and usability without sacrificing faithfulness.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.41856v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conversational explainable AI (ConvXAI) agents often use GUS-style architectures with separate modules for intent recognition, dialogue management, and template-based response generation. While faithful to the underlying XAI methods, these pipelines are hard to adapt and often struggle with context-dependent follow-up questions. We present SimXAI, a lightweight LLM-centric conversational layer that replaces these modules with a single tool-calling LLM that bridges access to existing XAI resources. Rather than a standalone agent, SimXAI serves as a modular interface that enables conversational access to external XAI resources. We further introduce an evaluation suite for single- and multi-turn parsing, faithfulness, and contextualization. Across existing and new datasets, SimXAI achieves strong function-selection accuracy and high faithfulness while better handling context-dependent requests. In a user study replacing only the conversational layer of TalkToModel, a representative GUS-based agent, users completed tasks more accurately and in fewer turn. Overall, SimXAI improves GUS-based design while preserving faithfulness and improving conversational quality.

items.title: Researchers propose TIZSKT for zero-shot cross-domain knowledge tracing using text as an index to predict student responses without target-domain training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Text as an Index for Zero-Shot Cross-Domain Knowledge Tracing
items.summary:
Researchers introduce TIZSKT, a method for zero-shot cross-domain knowledge tracing that predicts a student's next response using question texts and behavioral history without requiring target-domain training data. The approach separates behavioral sequence modeling from domain-specific evidence construction, employing a frozen text encoder and unsupervised projections to create fixed question addresses that aggregate historical correctness summaries.

TIZSKT incorporates components such as the Mastery-Dynamics Encoder, Text-Addressing Kernel, Cross-Segment Continuation, and Evidence-Volume Read-Out to effectively model student performance across domains. Evaluations on three public datasets using leave-one-domain-out experiments show that TIZSKT outperforms existing baselines in mean AUC and accuracy, with ablation studies confirming the importance of text addressing and cross-segment continuation features.
